research_question: Does causal drift-directed probability redistribution across matched multi-timescale recursive least-squares experts reduce temporally ordered prequential scaled absolute error relative to constant fixed share on non-stationary real-world univariate forecasting tasks?
hypothesis: When recent ensemble loss rises above its slow baseline, reallocating fixed-share mass toward shorter-memory experts will adapt faster than uniform redistribution while preserving long-memory accuracy outside shifts.
hypothesis_revision_2: When a mode-independent causal mean expert-bank loss rises above its slow baseline, increasing share and directing it using memory length plus relative expert loss will adapt faster than matched uniform-target and constant-rate controls without sacrificing stable-regime accuracy.
falsifier: The hypothesis is not supported if the frozen confirmatory paired effect versus constant fixed share fails to exceed the practical threshold, its uncertainty interval includes no benefit, or predefined robustness slices reverse the effect.
contribution_boundary: The study does not claim novelty for expert aggregation, fixed share, time-varying Markov expert transitions, RLS, adaptive forgetting, drift detection, or adaptive conformal prediction individually. It tests one causal resource-light joint policy for adapting share rate and redistribution target; mechanism claims require the revision-2 isolating controls.
primary_endpoint: Paired mean difference in per-timestamp absolute error divided by the training seasonal-naive scale: MASE(DDFS) - MASE(constant fixed share). Lower is better.
practical_effect_threshold: At least 0.01 absolute MASE improvement and at least 1 percent relative improvement, both versus constant fixed share.
protected_boundary: Final temporal segment of each confirmatory series; no result may be inspected before the freeze receipt binds protocol, source, data manifest, splits, model configuration, statistics, and exclusions.
